title: Episode 319: Oliver Cromwell: The Lord Protector, the New Model Army, and the Commonwealth
description:
The electrifying, controversial life of Oliver Cromwell, the only commoner ever to rule England as head of state. A devout, melancholy Puritan farmer from Huntingdon, Cromwell was forty-three when the Civil War erupted, transforming overnight into a military genius of the cavalry. Commanding the Ironsides and forging the New Model Army, Cromwell orchestrated the execution of Charles I and abolished the monarchy to establish the English Republic. Waging brutal, controversial campaigns in Ireland and Scotland, Cromwell dissolved Parliament by force and assumed supreme power as Lord Protector. Refusing the crown, Cromwell built an uncrowned empire before his premature death unleashed the Restoration. Discover the Puritan Colossus.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, our Kings and Queens of England series examines the remarkable commoner who sat upon the seat of kings: a religious visionary, military genius, and polarizing ruler who governed an uncrowned British republic: Oliver Cromwell. Here is George with the extraordinary saga of the Lord Protector.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE HUNTINGDON FARMER: FAITH AND OBSCURITY: 1599 TO 1642
Born in April 1599 in the market town of Huntingdon in Cambridgeshire, Oliver Cromwell was a minor country gentleman descended from Thomas Cromwell's sister. Educated at Sidney Sussex College, Cambridge, Cromwell spent his twenties and thirties in obscurity, farming rye and raising sheep in the flat, misty fenlands of St. Ives and Ely. Tormented by severe bouts of hypochondriacal depression, Cromwell experienced a profound religious awakening in the early 1630s, embracing radical Puritanism with apocalyptic conviction, believing he was an instrument chosen by God's sovereign grace. Elected MP for Cambridge in the Short and Long Parliaments of 1640, Cromwell was described by Sir Philip Warwick as a rough, slovenly figure dressed in a plain cloth suit made by an ill country tailor, with a red, swollen face and a sharp, untuneable voice that thundered against bishops. When civil war broke out in August 1642, forty-three-year-old Cromwell possessed zero military experience. Yet within months, he raised a troop of sixty Cambridge yeomen horsemen, demanding men of deep religious faith who 'made some conscience of what they did', laying the foundation for the most formidable cavalry regiment in Europe. Cromwell's early years in Huntingdon and St. Ives were marked by intense spiritual anguish, wrestling with Calvinist doctrines of predestination and eternal damnation. He frequently summoned his physician, Sir Theodore de Mayerne, in the middle of the night, convinced he was dying of spleen or heart failure. When his spiritual breakthrough occurred, it was an explosion of ecstatic certainty: Cromwell believed that God had personally justified him, filling his soul with divine light. This profound inner conviction made Cromwell an unstoppable force on the political and battlefield stage: he never doubted that his military victories were direct, unmistakable confirmations of God's providential favor upon his holy mission.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE IRONSIDES AND THE NEW MODEL ARMY: MARSTON MOOR AND NASEBY
Cromwell's tactical brilliance revolutionized seventeenth-century warfare: while Royalist cavalry under Prince Rupert scattered in disorganized pursuits to pillage, Cromwell trained his Puritans—dubbed 'Ironsides'—to charge at a steady, cohesive trot, strike like a sledgehammer, wheel in tight formation, and regroup immediately for secondary charges. At the Battle of Marston Moor in July 1644, on a rain-swept Yorkshire moor, Cromwell's cavalry shattered Rupert's cavalry and routed the Royalist army, killing four thousand men. Cromwell famously wrote: 'It had all the evidences of an absolute victory obtained by the Lord's blessing upon the Godly Party principally... God made them as stubble to our swords.' Frustrated by aristocratic parliamentary commanders who hesitated to defeat the king completely, Cromwell championed the Self-Denying Ordinance and the creation of the New Model Army in 1645. Clad in red coats and singing psalms as they advanced, the New Model Army was the world's first modern professional army, annihilating Royalist armies at Naseby and Langport. The New Model Army was unlike any fighting force European Christendom had ever witnessed: promotions were based strictly on military capability and godly zeal rather than aristocratic bloodlines. Soldiers carried copies of the 'Souldier's Pocket Bible' in their tunic pockets, engaged in theological debates in camp, and were forbidden from swearing, drunkenness, or plundering on pain of severe whipping or execution. At the Battle of Marston Moor, when Prince Rupert asked an English prisoner whether Cromwell was in the field, calling him 'Ironside', Rupert coined the moniker that would strike terror into Royalist hearts from Cornwall to the Scottish Highlands.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: REGICIDE: CONDEMNING THE KING: 1647 TO 1649
Following the King's defeat, Cromwell initially sought an honorable constitutional settlement, negotiating with Charles I at Hampton Court to preserve a limited monarchy and religious liberty. But Charles's treacherous secret treaty with the Scots to launch the Second Civil War convinced Cromwell that the King was a hardened hypocrite who had invited foreign invasion upon his own people. During a three-day prayer meeting of the Army at Windsor Castle in April 1648, Cromwell and his officers wept in theological agony, resolving that it was their holy duty 'to call Charles Stuart, that man of blood, to an account for the blood he had shed'. Following Pride's Purge in December 1648, Cromwell drove the regicide forward with iron resolve, telling hesitating judges: 'I tell you we will cut off his head with the crown upon it.' When Charles was beheaded on January 30, 1649, Cromwell viewed the event not as a political coup, but as a terrifying, righteous judgment of God against a perjured ruler. During the Army Debates at St. Mary's Church in Putney in the autumn of 1647, Cromwell faced radical ideological currents from the Levellers within his own ranks. Men like Colonel Thomas Rainsborough argued for universal male suffrage, famously declaring: 'The poorest he that is in England hath a life to live as the greatest he.' Cromwell fiercely resisted such radical democracy, arguing that extending the vote to propertyless men would destroy all social order and property rights. Yet when the King reignited the Civil War, Cromwell became radicalized: convinced that Charles was a murderer who had broken his covenant with God, Cromwell drove the King's trial forward with relentless, terrifying determination.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE CONQUEST OF IRELAND: DROGHEDA AND WEXFORD: 1649 TO 1650
In August 1649, Cromwell landed in Ireland with twelve thousand veteran soldiers to suppress a Royalist and Catholic confederacy. What followed remains the darkest and most bitterly contested chapter of his career. In September 1649, Cromwell besieged the royalist-held walled town of Drogheda on the River Boyne. When the garrison rejected his summons to surrender, Cromwell ordered an immediate storming, ordering that no quarter be given to anyone found in arms. Over three thousand Royalist soldiers, along with Catholic priests and friars, were massacred in cold blood, with Cromwell recording in his official dispatch: 'I am persuaded that this is a righteous judgment of God upon these barbarous wretches.' A similar massacre occurred weeks later at Wexford. The subsequent Cromwellian Settlement confiscated millions of acres of Catholic-owned land, banishing native Irish landowners to the stony barrens of Connacht under the chilling ultimatum: 'To Hell or Connacht!' Cromwell's name became permanently synonymous in Irish history with ruthless devastation, sectarian slaughter, and colonial dispossession. The horrors of the siege of Drogheda in September 1649 cast an indelible, dark shadow across Cromwell's legacy. After the New Model Army breached the medieval stone walls, Royalist defenders took refuge in the wooden tower of St. Peter's Church; Cromwell ordered the church set on fire, recording that he heard one soldier shouting from the flames: 'God damn me, God confound me; I burn, I burn!' The massacre of the garrison and Catholic clergy was justified by Cromwell as a proportionate retribution for the Irish rebellion of 1641, yet it remains one of the most brutal war crimes of the early modern era, leaving scars of sectarian bitterness that plagued Anglo-Irish relations for over three centuries.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: DUNBAR, WORCESTER, AND THE RUMP PARLIAMENT EXPULSION: 1650 TO 1653
Rushing to Scotland in 1650, where Charles II had signed the Covenant and raised a Scottish army, Cromwell achieved his tactical masterpiece at the Battle of Dunbar in September 1650. Cornered on a narrow coastal strip between the Lammermuir Hills and the North Sea, outnumbered two to one, Cromwell launched a surprise dawn attack around the Scottish flank. As the sun broke over the sea, Cromwell shouted: 'Let God arise, and let his enemies be scattered!' The Scottish army was destroyed. Exactly one year later, on September 3, 1651, Cromwell crushed Charles II's final invasion army at Worcester, ending nine years of civil war, with Charles II fleeing into foreign exile after hiding in the branches of the Royal Oak at Boscobel. Returning to London, Cromwell grew disgusted by the corrupt, self-serving MPs of the Rump Parliament who delayed fresh elections. On April 20, 1653, Cromwell marched into the House of Commons with forty musketeers, shouting at the MPs: 'You have sat too long for any good you have been doing lately... In the name of God, go!' He pointed to the Speaker's golden mace, sneering: 'What shall we do with this bauble? Take it away!' Locking the doors, Cromwell established an uncrowned military protectorate. At the Battle of Dunbar in September 1650, Cromwell was trapped in a seemingly hopeless tactical predicament, his army decimated by dysentery and winter rains. When the Scottish general David Leslie descended from the high ground of Doon Hill to cut off Cromwell's retreat, Cromwell saw the tactical mistake and exclaimed: 'The Lord hath delivered them into our hands!' In the pre-dawn darkness, Cromwell hurled his cavalry around the Scottish right, rolling up the Scottish army in one hour. When he dissolved the Rump Parliament in 1653, Cromwell was beside himself with fury: pointing at prominent corrupt members, he shouted that one was a whoremaster, another an adulterer, and another a glutton, ending the last vestige of parliamentary democracy with the butt ends of muskets.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE LORD PROTECTOR AND THE RULE OF THE MAJOR-GENERALS: 1653 TO 1657
In December 1653, under England's first and only written constitution, the Instrument of Government, fifty-four-year-old Oliver Cromwell was sworn in as Lord Protector of the Commonwealth of England, Scotland, and Ireland. Dressed in a plain black velvet coat, he held greater sovereign power than any Tudor king. He readmitted Jews to England after three hundred and sixty-five years of banishment since Edward I, granted unprecedented religious liberty to Protestant sects, and built an invincible navy under Robert Blake that defeated the Dutch and captured Jamaica from Spain. But domestic governance proved authoritarian: in 1655, following Royalist uprisings, Cromwell divided England into eleven military districts governed by Puritan Major-Generals. Alehouses and theaters were shuttered, horse racing and bear-baiting banned, and even the celebration of Christmas was outlawed as a pagan feast. In 1657, when Parliament presented the Humble Petition and Advice offering Cromwell the royal crown of England, the Lord Protector wrestled with his conscience for weeks before refusing, declaring that God had blasted the title of king and he would not set up what Providence had cast down. The Rule of the Major-Generals in 1655 transformed England into an austere, joyless military dictatorship that traumatized the national consciousness. Puritan soldiers smashed maypoles, shut down theaters, fined citizens for swearing in public, and enforced strict Sabbath observance where even walking for pleasure on Sunday was penalized. Soldiers went through London streets on Christmas Day, entering private homes to confiscate roasting geese and plum puddings, decrying the feast as a popish abomination. The deep English revulsion against standing armies, military rule, and religious fanaticism originated in the oppressive, suffocating years of Cromwell's Major-Generals.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE GREAT STORM, DEATH, AND THE TYBURN EXHUMATION: 1658 TO 1661
In August 1658, Cromwell's iron health cracked following the agonizing death of his beloved daughter, Elizabeth Claypole. Ravaged by malarial ague and kidney stones at Whitehall Palace, fifty-nine-year-old Cromwell took to his deathbed. On the night of September 2, 1658, a terrifying, hurricane-force gale swept across England, uprooting ancient oaks and tearing roofs from churches—a tempest remembered as 'Oliver's Wind'. On the afternoon of Friday, September 3, the anniversary of his victories at Dunbar and Worcester, Oliver Cromwell died. He was given a colossal state funeral in Westminster Abbey, his wax effigy crowned with an imperial diadem. But the Commonwealth could not survive without its giant: his son Richard Cromwell, dubbed 'Tumbledown Dick', resigned within eight months, and in May 1660, Charles II was restored to the throne. In January 1661, on the twelfth anniversary of Charles I's execution, the Royalists exhumed Cromwell's corpse from Westminster Abbey. Dragged through London to Tyburn, the dead Protector's body was hung in chains on the gallows, beheaded, and his severed head impaled upon a twenty-foot spike atop Westminster Hall, where it stood in the wind and rain for twenty-five years. The bizarre, posthumous execution of Cromwell's corpse in January 1661 revealed the venomous fury of the restored Royalists. After hanging at Tyburn gallows from sunrise to sunset, the executioner hacked off the embalmed head with eight blows of an ax. The head was impaled on a high iron spike above the south roof of Westminster Hall, where it remained through sun, snow, and gales until blown down during a Great Storm in 1703, picked up by a sentry and passed through private collections of curiosities for over two centuries. Finally, in 1960, the severed head of Oliver Cromwell was reverently interred in an unmarked grave near the ante-chapel of Sidney Sussex College, Cambridge, where the Lord Protector had studied as a youth.
